payload.title: Ambition and Belonging

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
In many works of fiction, a character's ambition becomes the engine that carries them out of the place, family, or community that made them. The pull may take the form of a scholarship that sends a child away from a village dialect, a business that rises while old friendships thin, or a talent that earns applause from strangers and suspicion at home. Ambition in such works is rarely simply admirable or simply corrupting. The same drive that frees a character can also strand them, and the success they reach for may cost the very belonging that once gave their striving its meaning.

Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which a character's ambition draws them toward success while separating them from a family, community, or place to which they once belonged. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the tension between the character's ambition and their sense of belonging contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.

Your essay should:
- State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
- Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Do not merely summarize the plot.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

Works you may choose from (or choose another work of fiction you know well):
- A Doll's House, Henrik Ibsen
- To the Lighthouse, Virginia Woolf
- Invisible Man, Ralph Ellison
- The Metamorphosis, Franz Kafka

- Jane Eyre, Charlotte Bronte

parts.model_answer:
When Pip finds out he has "great expectations," the news seems like a way out of the marshes, the forge, and a life he has already learned to be ashamed of. Charles Dickens doesn't treat Pip's ambition as simply a mistake, though. In Great Expectations the drive to become a gentleman really does pull Pip out of a cramped, sometimes cruel home, but it also teaches him to see the people who loved him through the eyes of the people who looked down on him. The novel suggests that ambition built on shame cuts a person off from belonging, and that the only success worth having is the one Pip finds at the end, when he is poor and humbled and able to go back home.

Pip's ambition starts as a wound, not a dream. At Satis House, Estella mocks his coarse hands and thick boots, and Miss Havisham watches it happen. Before this visit Pip had no reason to think the forge was low. Afterward he can't stop seeing it as low. Dickens makes the point that ambition can be planted from outside: Pip's longing to rise comes from humiliation by a class that has no real affection for him. That is why it divides him from Joe so quickly. Once he wants Estella's approval, he has to hold Joe in contempt, even though Joe is the one adult who protected him from Mrs. Joe's rages.

The clearest picture of this split is Joe's visit to London. Joe, uncomfortable in his good clothes, keeps calling Pip "sir," and his hat keeps sliding off the mantel while Pip winces and wishes he would leave. The scene is funny, but it hurts, because the comedy is told from inside Pip's embarrassment. The older Pip narrating the story knows how badly he acted, and that double vision matters. We see the young man's snobbery and the grown man's regret together, so the scene shows both what ambition has gotten Pip, polish and a place in London, and what it has cost him, the ease of simply being loved. Joe gets this better than Pip does. He leaves saying, in effect, that they belong in different places now, and it sounds less like an insult than like grief.

Someone could argue that Pip owed nothing to the marsh community, which wasn't much of a community. Mrs. Joe raises him "by hand" and treats him like a burden, Pumblechook bullies him, and Orlick is dangerous. That objection has some force, and Dickens doesn't make the village into paradise. But Joe and Biddy are a different kind of belonging, one based on loyalty instead of status, and the plot tests which kind is real. The twist that Magwitch, not Miss Havisham, is Pip's benefactor wrecks the fantasy that Pip's rise was refined or deserved. His gentility was paid for by a transported convict, the same man he fed on the marshes as a frightened child. In this way the structure of the novel drags Pip's ambition back to the place it was trying to escape. The marshes were never really behind him.

This is why the ending works as a return and not just as a punishment. Pip learns to love Magwitch and stays loyal to him as he dies, which is the first time he chooses a bond over appearances. Then Pip falls ill, and it is Joe who nurses him and quietly pays his debts. Pip goes back intending to propose to Biddy and finds she has married Joe, so he can't simply step back into the old life either. He works abroad with Herbert and earns a modest living by honest labor. Dickens doesn't give him the triumph he wanted, or a full homecoming. What Pip gets is the self-knowledge that lets him tell the story the way he does: an ambition that once separated him from belonging becomes, in hindsight, the way he learns what belonging was worth.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis names a work and makes a claim about how the tension between ambition and belonging shapes the meaning of the work as a whole, for example that a novel shows upward mobility turning into exile. Restating the prompt, saying only that a character is ambitious and loses friends, or giving a claim with no interpretation does not earn the point. The thesis may appear anywhere and may be more than one sentence.

Strong responses pick specific moments, such as a departure, a changed way of speaking, an awkward reunion, or a final image of isolation, and explain how each one shows both what ambition gains and what belonging loses. Commentary should tie these moments to an interpretation of the whole work rather than to the character's psychology alone. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific evidence and a line of reasoning that develops. A score of 2 fits responses that mostly summarize the plot with general comments. A score of 3 fits accurate but uneven analysis that only sometimes links evidence to the thesis.

Sophistication can show up as a sustained account of the double edge: weighing whether the lost community deserved loyalty, placing the character's choice within social or historical pressures, or showing how the work's structure, such as its return or its ending, complicates the thesis. One passing nod to complexity, or ornate wording, does not earn the point.

Commentary should tie these moments to an interpretation of the whole work rather than to the character's psychology alone. One passing nod to complexity, or ornate wording, does not earn the point.

- Row A: "The novel suggests that ambition built on shame cuts a person off from belonging, and that the only success worth having is the one Pip finds at the end" - A defensible thesis that interprets the whole work. It goes beyond saying Pip is ambitious and loses Joe: it names where the ambition comes from (shame) and makes a claim about what counts as success in the novel, which sets up the line of reasoning from Satis House to London to the ending.
- Row B: "Dickens makes the point that ambition can be planted from outside" - Commentary goes past summary. The Satis House evidence (coarse hands, thick boots) is used to explain why the ambition separates Pip from Joe, so the evidence connects back to the thesis about shame.
- Row B: "The older Pip narrating the story knows how badly he acted, and that double vision matters." - Looks at a second literary element, retrospective first-person narration, and explains how it lets one scene show both the gain and the loss. This kind of analysis of multiple techniques is what a 4 in Row B calls for.
- Row B: "In this way the structure of the novel drags Pip's ambition back to the place it was trying to escape." - Uses plot structure (the Magwitch reveal) as a technique and ties it to the interpretation of the whole work, not just to Pip's psychology. Each body paragraph builds on the last, so the line of reasoning develops.
- Row C: "Someone could argue that Pip owed nothing to the marsh community, which wasn't much of a community." - Takes on an alternative reading, whether the lost community deserved loyalty, with specific evidence (Mrs. Joe, Pumblechook, Orlick) and then refines the argument by separating loyalty-based belonging from status. This is real engagement, not a passing nod.
- Row C: "so he can't simply step back into the old life either" - Keeps the complexity going into the conclusion by showing how the ending complicates a simple return-home reading. The double edge of ambition stays in view across the essay, which supports the sophistication point.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In The Great Gatsby, F. Scott Fitzgerald shows that Jay Gatsby's ambition to become somebody carries him away from the people and place that made him, and that this success leaves him with nothing to belong to. Gatsby's rise is therefore less a triumph than a kind of exile, and the novel uses it to question whether the American dream can ever really be reached.

Gatsby begins as James Gatz, the son of poor farming people in North Dakota, and he decides at a young age to invent a new self. When he meets Dan Cody he leaves his family behind and takes a new name, so his ambition requires cutting off where he came from. This shows that for Gatsby success means escaping his origins rather than building on them. Later, he tells Nick a story about being from a wealthy family in the Midwest, which is a lie meant to hide his real background. The fact that he has to lie about his past shows that the belonging he lost was never replaced by anything real.

Gatsby's house in West Egg is another example. He becomes extremely rich and throws huge parties, but the guests mostly do not know him and come only for the free drinks and entertainment. Nick notices that people gossip about Gatsby without caring about him. The crowds are large, but Gatsby stands apart and watches, so Fitzgerald is showing that his money has bought attention but not community. Even more, West Egg is separated from East Egg, where Daisy lives, by the bay, and this geography shows how Gatsby can see what he wants but cannot truly join it. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this, because it is always visible but out of reach. Gatsby's ambition is really aimed at Daisy and the old-money world she represents, and that world never accepts him, as shown when Tom exposes him in the hotel scene.

The ending of the novel makes the tension clearest. After Gatsby is killed, almost nobody comes to his funeral, and the people from his parties do not appear. The only family member who comes is his father, who is proud of his son's success, which is a sad contrast with how Gatsby had hidden his family. This moment suggests that the belonging Gatsby gave up was the only kind that was left to him at the end. Nick, who narrates, is from the Midwest too, and he decides to go back, which implies that the novel sees some value in the place Gatsby ran from.

Overall, Fitzgerald presents Gatsby's ambition as both admirable and tragic. His dream is a hopeful one, but it costs him his roots and leaves him alone, which makes the novel a warning about success that is cut off from belonging.
- Row A: "Gatsby's rise is therefore less a triumph than a kind of exile" - This is a defensible thesis that names the work and claims ambition turns into exile, tied to a view of the American dream. It earns the thesis point, though it is stated fairly broadly.
- Row B: "When he meets Dan Cody he leaves his family behind and takes a new name" - This is a specific, accurate moment that links ambition to loss of belonging. The commentary stays general, though, and does not discuss how the renaming works as a technique.
- Row B: "The crowds are large, but Gatsby stands apart and watches" - This is relevant evidence from the parties, and the commentary explains that money bought attention but not community. It is only loosely specific, with no concrete detail from a particular scene.
- Row B: "The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this" - This names a symbol and connects it to the idea of reaching without belonging, which gets some credit for technique. The explanation is thin and repeats the earlier geography point.
- Row B: "The only family member who comes is his father" - This is accurate ending evidence tied to the thesis. The comment about the father is somewhat muddled and the analysis stops short of developing it.
- Row C: "which implies that the novel sees some value in the place Gatsby ran from" - This gestures at a complication, that the novel may value the Midwest, but it is a passing remark and not sustained. The essay never weighs whether the lost community deserved loyalty, so sophistication is not earned.

Sample essay (low; scored 2/6: thesis 0, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald, Jay Gatsby is a very ambitious character who wants to be successful and rich. His ambition makes him leave his family and the place he came from, and this shows that ambition can be both good and bad.

Gatsby starts out as James Gatz from North Dakota who has poor farmer parents. He changes his name and becomes Jay Gatsby because he wants to be someone better. He meets Dan Cody and learns about wealthy life. This is the start of him leaving his past behind. Later he becomes rich through bootlegging and buys a huge mansion in West Egg across the water from Daisy. He throws big parties every weekend with lots of people who come but do not really know him. This shows he is successful but he is also alone.

Nick Carraway narrates the story and he sees how Gatsby is different from the other people. Gatsby has the green light at the end of Daisy's dock which he reaches for. The green light is a symbol of his dream. Even though he has money he cannot get Daisy back because she is from old money and he is not. Gatsby's ambition makes him successful but it does not give him belonging.

At the end of the book Gatsby is killed in his pool and almost nobody comes to his funeral. His father Henry Gatz comes from the Midwest. This shows that Gatsby lost his family and community because of his ambition. In conclusion, Gatsby's ambition shows that success can cost a person everything they belonged to.
- Row A: "His ambition makes him leave his family and the place he came from, and this shows that ambition can be both good and bad." - Names the work and gestures at the double edge, but the claim is vague and never says what the novel as a whole means by it. Not a developed interpretation, so the thesis point is doubtful.
- Row B: "Gatsby starts out as James Gatz from North Dakota who has poor farmer parents." - Accurate detail, but it is plot summary. It is not tied to what belonging is lost or how the text presents it.
- Row B: "The green light is a symbol of his dream." - Identifies a symbol but does not explain how it shapes meaning or links ambition to lost belonging. A general statement rather than commentary.
- Row B: "almost nobody comes to his funeral" - A relevant final image of isolation, but the commentary just restates that he lost his community instead of analyzing the ending's effect on the whole work.
- Row C: "In conclusion, Gatsby's ambition shows that success can cost a person everything they belonged to." - Generic conclusion that oversimplifies. It does not weigh whether Gatsby's past or the Buchanans' world deserved loyalty, or consider social context, so no sophistication.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis names a work and makes a claim about how the tension between ambition and belonging shapes the meaning of the work as a whole, for example that a novel shows upward mobility turning into exile. The thesis may appear anywhere and may be more than one sentence.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses pick specific moments, such as a departure, a changed way of speaking, an awkward reunion, or a final image of isolation, and explain how each one shows both what ambition gains and what belonging loses. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific evidence and a line of reasoning that develops. A score of 2 fits responses that mostly summarize the plot with general comments. A score of 3 fits accurate but uneven analysis that only sometimes links evidence to the thesis.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

lines_of_reasoning: Ambition as tragic self-destruction: the climb isolates the character until success is hollow (Macbeth; The Great Gatsby).
Ambition as necessary escape from a confining community, with belonging shown as partly oppressive (Jane Eyre; Brooklyn by Toibin; A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man).
The social system as the true culprit, forcing a choice between mobility and loyalty (Great Expectations; Things Fall Apart, through Nwoye and Okonkwo; The Namesake).
Ambition reshaping language and manners so the character becomes a stranger at home (Great Expectations; Pygmalion, if drama is permitted; Educated is nonfiction and should not be used).
Ambition revealed as a search for belonging in a new place, which itself fails (The Great Gatsby; Sister Carrie; Native Son).
A return home that tests whether belonging can be recovered (Pip's return to Joe; The Remains of the Day; Season of Migration to the North).
Ambition belonging to a family and placed on a child, so success and belonging are tangled rather than opposed (The Joy Luck Club; Death of a Salesman; A Fine Balance).
defensible_positions: The work suggests ambition is worth its cost because the original community could not accommodate the self.
The work condemns ambition by showing that success without belonging is empty.
The work refuses to resolve the tension, showing that the character can neither fully rise nor fully return.
The work blames social structures, not individual desire, for making ambition and belonging incompatible.
common_pitfalls: Retelling the plot of the character's rise without explaining what the work suggests about ambition.
Treating ambition as only good or only bad without addressing the double-edged nature the prompt sets up.
Forcing a work to fit, such as choosing a character with ambition but no meaningful loss of belonging.
Discussing ambition in general life terms rather than analyzing the chosen work.
Choosing nonfiction, film, or a work without enough detail remembered to support specific claims.

It goes beyond saying Pip is ambitious and loses Joe: it names where the ambition comes from (shame) and makes a claim about what counts as success in the novel, which sets up the line of reasoning from Satis House to London to the ending.

annotations.quote: Dickens makes the point that ambition can be planted from outside
annotations.comment: Commentary goes past summary. The Satis House evidence (coarse hands, thick boots) is used to explain why the ambition separates Pip from Joe, so the evidence connects back to the thesis about shame.

annotations.quote: The older Pip narrating the story knows how badly he acted, and that double vision matters.
annotations.comment: Looks at a second literary element, retrospective first-person narration, and explains how it lets one scene show both the gain and the loss. This kind of analysis of multiple techniques is what a 4 in Row B calls for.

annotations.quote: In this way the structure of the novel drags Pip's ambition back to the place it was trying to escape.
annotations.comment: Uses plot structure (the Magwitch reveal) as a technique and ties it to the interpretation of the whole work, not just to Pip's psychology. Each body paragraph builds on the last, so the line of reasoning develops.

annotations.quote: Someone could argue that Pip owed nothing to the marsh community, which wasn't much of a community.
annotations.comment: Takes on an alternative reading, whether the lost community deserved loyalty, with specific evidence (Mrs. Joe, Pumblechook, Orlick) and then refines the argument by separating loyalty-based belonging from status. This is real engagement, not a passing nod.

annotations.quote: so he can't simply step back into the old life either
annotations.comment: Keeps the complexity going into the conclusion by showing how the ending complicates a simple return-home reading. The double edge of ambition stays in view across the essay, which supports the sophistication point.

samples.essay:
In The Great Gatsby, F. Scott Fitzgerald shows that Jay Gatsby's ambition to become somebody carries him away from the people and place that made him, and that this success leaves him with nothing to belong to. Gatsby's rise is therefore less a triumph than a kind of exile, and the novel uses it to question whether the American dream can ever really be reached.

Gatsby begins as James Gatz, the son of poor farming people in North Dakota, and he decides at a young age to invent a new self. When he meets Dan Cody he leaves his family behind and takes a new name, so his ambition requires cutting off where he came from. This shows that for Gatsby success means escaping his origins rather than building on them. Later, he tells Nick a story about being from a wealthy family in the Midwest, which is a lie meant to hide his real background. The fact that he has to lie about his past shows that the belonging he lost was never replaced by anything real.

Gatsby's house in West Egg is another example. He becomes extremely rich and throws huge parties, but the guests mostly do not know him and come only for the free drinks and entertainment. Nick notices that people gossip about Gatsby without caring about him. The crowds are large, but Gatsby stands apart and watches, so Fitzgerald is showing that his money has bought attention but not community. Even more, West Egg is separated from East Egg, where Daisy lives, by the bay, and this geography shows how Gatsby can see what he wants but cannot truly join it. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this, because it is always visible but out of reach. Gatsby's ambition is really aimed at Daisy and the old-money world she represents, and that world never accepts him, as shown when Tom exposes him in the hotel scene.

The ending of the novel makes the tension clearest. After Gatsby is killed, almost nobody comes to his funeral, and the people from his parties do not appear. The only family member who comes is his father, who is proud of his son's success, which is a sad contrast with how Gatsby had hidden his family. This moment suggests that the belonging Gatsby gave up was the only kind that was left to him at the end. Nick, who narrates, is from the Midwest too, and he decides to go back, which implies that the novel sees some value in the place Gatsby ran from.

Overall, Fitzgerald presents Gatsby's ambition as both admirable and tragic. His dream is a hopeful one, but it costs him his roots and leaves him alone, which makes the novel a warning about success that is cut off from belonging.

annotations.quote: Gatsby's rise is therefore less a triumph than a kind of exile
annotations.comment: This is a defensible thesis that names the work and claims ambition turns into exile, tied to a view of the American dream. It earns the thesis point, though it is stated fairly broadly.

annotations.quote: When he meets Dan Cody he leaves his family behind and takes a new name
annotations.comment: This is a specific, accurate moment that links ambition to loss of belonging. The commentary stays general, though, and does not discuss how the renaming works as a technique.

annotations.quote: The crowds are large, but Gatsby stands apart and watches
annotations.comment: This is relevant evidence from the parties, and the commentary explains that money bought attention but not community. It is only loosely specific, with no concrete detail from a particular scene.

annotations.quote: The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this
annotations.comment: This names a symbol and connects it to the idea of reaching without belonging, which gets some credit for technique. The explanation is thin and repeats the earlier geography point.

annotations.quote: The only family member who comes is his father
annotations.comment: This is accurate ending evidence tied to the thesis. The comment about the father is somewhat muddled and the analysis stops short of developing it.

annotations.quote: which implies that the novel sees some value in the place Gatsby ran from
annotations.comment: This gestures at a complication, that the novel may value the Midwest, but it is a passing remark and not sustained. The essay never weighs whether the lost community deserved loyalty, so sophistication is not earned.

samples.essay:
In The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald, Jay Gatsby is a very ambitious character who wants to be successful and rich. His ambition makes him leave his family and the place he came from, and this shows that ambition can be both good and bad.

Gatsby starts out as James Gatz from North Dakota who has poor farmer parents. He changes his name and becomes Jay Gatsby because he wants to be someone better. He meets Dan Cody and learns about wealthy life. This is the start of him leaving his past behind. Later he becomes rich through bootlegging and buys a huge mansion in West Egg across the water from Daisy. He throws big parties every weekend with lots of people who come but do not really know him. This shows he is successful but he is also alone.

Nick Carraway narrates the story and he sees how Gatsby is different from the other people. Gatsby has the green light at the end of Daisy's dock which he reaches for. The green light is a symbol of his dream. Even though he has money he cannot get Daisy back because she is from old money and he is not. Gatsby's ambition makes him successful but it does not give him belonging.

At the end of the book Gatsby is killed in his pool and almost nobody comes to his funeral. His father Henry Gatz comes from the Midwest. This shows that Gatsby lost his family and community because of his ambition. In conclusion, Gatsby's ambition shows that success can cost a person everything they belonged to.

annotations.quote: His ambition makes him leave his family and the place he came from, and this shows that ambition can be both good and bad.
annotations.comment: Names the work and gestures at the double edge, but the claim is vague and never says what the novel as a whole means by it. Not a developed interpretation, so the thesis point is doubtful.

annotations.quote: Gatsby starts out as James Gatz from North Dakota who has poor farmer parents.
annotations.comment: Accurate detail, but it is plot summary. It is not tied to what belonging is lost or how the text presents it.

annotations.quote: The green light is a symbol of his dream.
annotations.comment: Identifies a symbol but does not explain how it shapes meaning or links ambition to lost belonging. A general statement rather than commentary.

annotations.quote: almost nobody comes to his funeral
annotations.comment: A relevant final image of isolation, but the commentary just restates that he lost his community instead of analyzing the ending's effect on the whole work.

annotations.quote: In conclusion, Gatsby's ambition shows that success can cost a person everything they belonged to.
annotations.comment: Generic conclusion that oversimplifies. It does not weigh whether Gatsby's past or the Buchanans' world deserved loyalty, or consider social context, so no sophistication.

blueprint.concept: ambition as a force that grants success while eroding belonging
blueprint.central_idea: Ambition is double-edged: it liberates a character from limits imposed by origin but can sever the ties that give identity and purpose.
blueprint.complexity: Works may present the loss as tragic, as necessary, as self-deception, or as a critique of the society that forces the choice between rising and belonging.
